analysis.one_liner: Gives the government power to force recalls of contaminated meat, poultry, and food and fine violators.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2006 and sent to two House committees but never got a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law at the time, the Agriculture Department could not force a meat or poultry company to recall contaminated products; it could only ask, and companies did most recalls voluntarily. This bill would have required anyone in the food supply chain who suspected their products were contaminated or mislabeled to tell the government, and would have let the Agriculture and Health and Human Services secretaries order recalls, pull inspectors from repeat-violation plants, and impose civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation ($500,000 for companies under the food provisions), with each day of a continuing violation counted separately.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers: contaminated meat, poultry, and other food would come off shelves faster because the government could order a recall instead of relying on a company's willingness to do it voluntarily. The bill also requires notice to consumers and state and local health officials about unsafe products, and lets the government suspend inspection at plants that willfully or repeatedly violate safety law, which stops their products from legally reaching the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who eats meat, poultry, or packaged food

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone other than a household consumer who has reason to believe a meat, poultry, or food product is adulterated or misbranded to notify the Secretary of Agriculture or Health and Human Services as soon as practicable [S2][S3].

Gives the Secretary of Agriculture authority for voluntary and mandatory recall and nondistribution of unsafe meat and poultry, including taking control of product and requiring companies to turn over distribution records so a recall can trace every buyer [S2][S3].

Gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services the same recall and notification authority over other food products, plus civil penalties of up to $100,000 for individuals and $500,000 for companies, with each day of a continuing violation a separate offense [S2][S3].

Lets the Secretary of Agriculture refuse or withdraw inspection from an establishment that commits willful or repeated violations, pending expedited hearing, which shuts down that establishment's legal sales [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and food manufacturers, distributors, and retailers would bear the cost of mandatory recalls, record-keeping for tracing distribution, notification duties, and potential fines. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices, and companies could face $100,000-per-violation penalties that accrue daily.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and food companies

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the government take control of a company's product and order recalls quickly, with an informal hearing required only within two business days after an order issues; affected businesses argued this shifts the burden onto them first and lets the agency decide later [S3].

Civil penalties can reach $100,000 per violation (up to $500,000 for companies on food provisions), counting each day of a continuing violation separately, so penalties can pile up fast on smaller firms even though the bill scales penalties by business size and violation history [S3].

The bill gives the Secretaries broad discretion ('as the Secretary determines to be necessary') over when consumers are notified and how recalls proceed, which businesses could see as unpredictable enforcement risk; judicial review is limited to the record the agency built [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill closes a real gap: at the time, meat and poultry recalls were voluntary, so the government could not compel a company to pull contaminated product, and it could not fine violators under these statutes. The costs fall mainly on companies that make or sell unsafe food, and the bill includes due process (hearings, judicial review, penalty caps, and penalty scaling by firm size). The main honest trade-off is faster, government-led recalls can mean larger or quicker recalls than a company would choose on its own, and compliance costs eventually show up in food prices. On balance it is a consumer-protection measure whose costs land on violators first.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees and their subcommittees from mid-2006 until that Congress ended in January 2007, and neither committee ever reported it for a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on June 29, 2006, with six Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, the House Energy and Commerce Committee, with provisions to be divided by jurisdiction [S5].

In July 2006 it was referred to the Agriculture Committee's Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee and the Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded, and the 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat, poultry, and food companies kept the pre-existing system, where recalls were voluntary and the government had no recall order or civil penalty authority over them. Consumers did not gain mandatory recall protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food and meat processors kept voluntary recalls

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; its sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, and opposition was inaction in committee rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended voluntary-only recalls for meat and subjected plants to mandatory recall orders, withdrawal of inspectors for repeat violations, and civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation. Its interest in keeping the voluntary system ran against faster removal of contaminated meat from shelves.
Same mandatory recall, inspection-withdrawal, and penalty provisions would have applied to poultry products under the Poultry Products Inspection Act amendments.

The bill imposed a notification duty on anyone handling suspect food, mandatory nondistribution and recall orders from HHS, and civil penalties up to $500,000 per violation per day for companies. Compliance and recall costs would have risen, with some passed to consumers in prices.
